#9869. Benchmarking Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus on 64 Broken Data Pipelines

Data engineer, 15+ years. IEEE Senior Member. Researching AI agents on data pipelines; building pipeverify. Writing about the bugs that pass

Data engineer, 15+ years. IEEE Senior Member. Researching AI agents on data pipelines; building pipeverify. Writing about the bugs that pass

Data engineer, 15+ years. IEEE Senior Member. Researching AI agents on data pipelines; building pipeverify. Writing about the bugs that pass

The phone buzzes. The nightly transactions job has failed again. You open the laptop, squint at the error, find the batch that came in twice, write a quick dedupe, rerun, watch it go green, and crawl back to bed.

Three days later finance asks why one region’s revenue is off.

If you’ve been in data engineering long enough, you’ve lived some version of that night. I’ve lived it for 15 years. So when teams started asking me whether they could hand that 2 a.m. page to an AI agent, I didn’t have a confident answer. And the question they always asked next was even harder: which model?

The small one is cheap and fast. The big one is supposedly smarter. Nobody wants to pay for the big one if the small one would do. I wanted a real answer, not a vibe. So I built a test and put three models on call: Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus.

The setup is a small card transaction pipeline: raw files land, three silver tables clean them, four gold tables aggregate them. Think of a typical medallion pipeline, shrunk down to run on a laptop with DuckDB.

I broke it 64 different ways, all things I’ve seen in production:

Twelve of the 64 have no safe fix from the evidence. The right answer there is to page a human and touch nothing.

Each model got what an on-call engineer would get: the error or the alerts, the pipeline SQL, a profile of every column, a few sample rows per batch, and the change notes from the source team. It had to answer with a decision (fix or escalate), a confidence score, and the SQL.

Then came the part most evaluations skip. I actually ran every proposed fix and compared every output table, row by row, with a clean build. A fix only counted if the data came out exactly right. “The job runs again” didn’t count.

Sonnet and Opus tied exactly, and Opus cost about four times as much to get there.

The relative cost is an index built from token counts and list-price ratios, so it’s only useful for comparing the three. It’s not a dollar figure.

All three knew when to stop. Every model escalated all 12 incidents that had no safe fix. None of them tried to be a hero on those, which honestly surprised me.

Opus wasn’t smarter here, just wordier. It wrote about 1,200 tokens per answer against Sonnet’s 260. Most of the extra cost is extra explanation, not extra correct fixes.

Sonnet and Opus missed the same two. Both escalated one seed of a merchant table with duplicate rows, because the evidence didn’t show whether the duplicates disagreed. Both also escalated one case of a lateness filter whose intent was unclear. I scored those as unnecessary, but I’d have been fine with a junior engineer making the same call.

Haiku failed in two different ways, and only one of them is cheap.

The cheap failure: it escalated 12 incidents it could have fixed. Mostly duplicate handling, account numbers that lost their leading zeros, and merchant IDs that gained a prefix. That costs a human some time, but no data gets hurt.

The expensive failure: two fixes that ran fine and produced wrong data.

That second one is the kind of fix that passes review. The dashboard looks right. The table underneath isn’t.

In real life, the source team doesn’t always tell you what changed. So I reran the 18 incidents that depended on a change note, with those notes removed. This is where the tiers finally separated.

Haiku halved its fix rate and escalated whenever the data didn’t explain itself. Sonnet dropped two, both on a partial time zone rollout.

Opus kept all 13. On the time zone case, it worked out from a handful of interleaved sample rows that one collector’s timestamps ran exactly six hours ahead of the other. No note told it that. It read the data.

So the honest answer to “is the expensive model worth it?” is: it depends on how well your organization documents its changes. With good change notes, Sonnet was enough. Without them, Opus was the only one that kept going. Writing better change notes might be cheaper than paying for the bigger model.

Remember the 2 a.m. dedupe from the start? One incident in the benchmark was exactly that night, and it fooled all three models the same way. Size didn’t help at all.

A batch arrived with duplicated transactions, and some copies carried different amounts. Nobody knew which amount was final. The only right move was to escalate.

I generated this incident twice with different random samples.

Same incident. Same models. Same prompt. The only thing that changed was which three rows happened to be in the sample. That was the whole difference between a safe page and quietly corrupted revenue. Not the model.

And here’s what really bothered me. I also ran 10 production-style data quality monitors after every fix: duplicate keys, volume against the 14-day median, nulls, reconciliation between tables, value domains and so on. Across 275 proposed fixes, those monitors never fired once. Not on the 5 fixes that corrupted data, not on anything.

That’s not a bug in my monitors. Monitors look for symptoms. A plausible fix removes the symptom. Keeping the wrong copy of a duplicate clears the duplicate-key alert just as well as keeping the right one. Monitors can tell you the data has a problem. They can’t tell you which of two clean-looking repairs is correct.

If I were putting an agent on data on-call tomorrow, here’s the setup the numbers point to.

That fourth point is what I’ve been building toward since. I turned that verification step into an open-source tool, pipeverify, that compares a table before and after a change, and against its raw source, and gives a PASS, REVIEW or BLOCK verdict in CI.

This is one synthetic pipeline, 64 cases, one model family, and one run per case. A difference of one or two incidents isn’t meaningful. The 0.65 threshold was tuned on the same data. Real incidents are messier than my evidence bundles. Treat this as a well-instrumented experiment, not a leaderboard.

Everything is public: the incidents, prompts, all 246 model responses and the scoring code.

So, can you hand the 2 a.m. page to an agent? Partly, yes. Pick a sensible model, let it say “I’m not sure,” and check its work against something it can’t fool. Just don’t let a green job convince you the data is fine. That’s the lesson I learned the hard way, years before any of these models existed.

If you’ve put an agent on a real pipeline, I’d love to hear what broke. That’s the data this benchmark

#9868. 9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Practical guidance on safer search, stronger login security, better executive protection, and other habits that help reduce enterprise risk.

9 Cybersecurity Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today’s Threats

Cybersecurity Awareness Month tends to bring no shortage of advice, but the most useful guidance for business readers is the kind that maps to the way attacks actually happen now: through everyday habits, trusted workflows, and small moments of inattention. Risks show up when employees trust a search result, follow a fake CAPTCHA prompt, scan a login QR code, click a social ad, reuse a weak recovery method, or assume that an AI model, executive device, or home network is secure by default. This article, compiled by the Dark Reading staff, and the accompanying videos bring those risks together in one place and focus on the practical behaviors and controls that can reduce them.

In October, a Dark Reading poll asked site visitors, "What's your biggest Cybersecurity Awareness Month challenge?" Readers identified phishing and social engineering as the top risk (39.1% of respondents), but that was neck-and-neck with shadow AI and risky data sharing (38.2%). A distant third was training fatigue and weak follow-through, identified as the top problem by 13.5% of respondents, and third-party and contractor access, with 9.2% of the vote.

Reader responses when asked, "What’s your biggest Cybersecurity Awareness Month challenge?" Source: Dark Reading

The following are nine tips that can move the dial on that enterprise risk in very real ways. A common thread for all of these is the fact that attackers win by abusing convenience, familiarity, and human trust, whether the issue is SEO poisoning, ClickFix, session hijacking, dark patterns, or dodgy ads on Facebook. That's why awareness training still matters, and why it shouldn't be a once-a-year affair but an everyday focus on a set of specific, repeatable habits backed by stronger enterprise safeguards.

For security leaders, that makes Cybersecurity Awareness Month a chance to do more than remind users to "be careful." It is an opportunity to push for better defaults: phishing-resistant MFA, tighter privilege controls, better reporting paths, safer browsing habits, stronger executive protection, and more realistic guidance for work that happens outside the office. The goal is to make the safe action the default action and to help employees recognize the red flags before a routine click becomes a business problem.

Embrace cybersecurity awareness in October and beyond with Dark Reading’s curated hub for security leaders — featuring expert news, analysis, and insights for hardening enterprise defenses in areas like identity security, AI risk, social engineering, supply chain, and more.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Becky Bracken, Media & Projects Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

As enterprises look to embrace agentic AI, they're sorting through frontier models, open-weight alternatives, and overseas offerings, and much of the focus is on evaluating the safeguards that, say, Claude might have vs. an open-weight alternative like Meta's Llama series. But for business leaders, the key question is not which model is inherently safe; it's whether your organization has put adequate controls around it. That means treating AI just like any other high-impact enterprise system that can be misconfigured, manipulated, abused, or compromised.

Every model type comes with tradeoffs. Frontier models may offer stronger vendor tooling, safety features, and governance support, but they can also introduce concentration and third-party risk. Open-weight models can give enterprises more transparency and control, but that control comes with more responsibility for hardening, patching, monitoring, and misuse prevention. Either way, the burden is on the enterprise.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the practical takeaway is to assume compromise and build from there. Security teams should treat model weights, code, training data, prompts, plugins, APIs, and downstream applications as one attack surface. Limit what models can access. Restrict permissions. Segment AI workloads from critical systems. Log activity aggressively. Test for prompt injection, data leakage, and identity abuse. And keep humans in the loop for consequential actions, especially where money, customer data, or operational decisions are involved.

This is a golden opportunity for cybersecurity teams to become business enablers in the best sense of the term. AI will move fast, vendors will keep promising better safeguards, and the market will keep generating noise. But the durable security advantage will come from steady internal discipline. AI models can help the business, but they cannot be trusted to protect the business.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Alex Culafi, Senior News Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

ClickFix is a simple but effective attack because it exploits something security teams deal with every day: people trying to solve a problem quickly. The user lands on a compromised or malicious website, a phishing page, or a fake browser-based meeting screen, and sees what looks like a normal verification or troubleshooting prompt.

But instead of asking them to check a box, the page tells them to open a system tool — often with Windows + R — and paste in a command that the site has already copied to their clipboard. Once they do, they can trigger the compromise themselves. Security researchers note that this technique has risen sharply and often relies on fake CAPTCHA or error messages that make the request seem routine.

No legitimate CAPTCHA, website, or meeting platform should ever ask a user to open Run, PowerShell, Terminal, or Command Prompt and paste in a script. A request like that should be treated as an immediate red flag. The attack works precisely because it looks like a harmless fix and can sidestep some browser-based protections by pushing the user to execute the command themselves.

Organizations should build this into awareness training now. Tell employees to stop immediately if a website asks them to copy-and-paste commands, press unusual key combinations, or "fix" an issue through a local system tool. Reinforce a simple rule: If a prompt moves from the browser into the operating system, assume it's suspicious until IT says otherwise. Also make it easy to report these incidents fast because early reporting can help security teams contain the damage and identify affected users quickly. Restricting access to system tools where appropriate can add another layer of defense.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Rob Wright, Senior News Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, here's a useful reminder for business leaders and employees alike: Treat social media ads as untrusted content. According to Gen Digital research, nearly one in three (31%) ads on Instagram and Facebook lead to scams, phishing pages, or malware.

And according to Reuters, Meta is charging higher premiums for advertisers that are considered risky. So not only have these platforms turned into a virtual minefield of scams, but Meta has a financial incentive to keep these ads online.

That matters because malicious ads often don't look malicious. They may mimic legitimate brands, use convincing creative, and point to spoofed URLs that appear credible at first glance. Even security-aware users can get caught. The real danger is that these ads exploit trust, urgency, and familiarity — exactly the tactics that work on busy professionals who are clicking quickly on personal devices outside the protections of corporate security tools.

The best defensive habit is simple: Do not click directly from social ads to make purchases, log in, or share payment information. If an offer looks legitimate, navigate to the brand's site manually, use a bookmarked link, or search for the company independently. Before entering credentials or card details, verify the domain carefully. Organizations should reinforce this behavior in security awareness training, especially for executives and remote workers who often blend personal and professional device use.

Caution remains the first line of defense. Encourage employees to use payment cards with fraud alerts, enable multifactor authentication on shopping and social accounts, and maintain healthy skepticism toward "limited-time" deals delivered through ad feeds.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Arielle Waldman, Features Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Ransomware has moved beyond encrypting systems and stealing data. Increasingly, attackers are pressuring organizations by targeting the people around their leaders: spouses, children, relatives, and close friends.

The "Semperis 2026 Ransomware Risk Report" found that 37% of attacks involved threats against employees' friends or family members. In other words, if attackers can't break your defenses fast enough, they may try to break your people instead. AI is accelerating this shift by making reconnaissance faster and cheaper, and threat actors can mine social media, public records, leaked data, and digital breadcrumbs to map relationships, impersonate trusted contacts, and build highly convincing social engineering campaigns.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, organizations should expand executive protection beyond the corporate perimeter. Start with digital footprint reduction: Encourage executives and family members to limit public exposure, remove unnecessary personal details from social profiles, and use aliases or less identifiable display names where practical. Establish family verification procedures, including safe words or challenge-response phrases, but rotate them regularly because any phrase used in a compromised channel should be treated as burned.

Most importantly, extend basic cyber hygiene to the household: Require strong unique passwords, enforce multifactor authentication on personal and shared accounts, secure home networks and connected devices, and train family members to recognize urgency-based scams, impersonation attempts, and suspicious contact. A child's gaming console, a spouse's reused password, or a relative's overshared profile can become the opening attackers need.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Fahmida Rashid, Editor-in-Chief at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Security awareness works better when it feels practical and relevant, not like a mandatory lecture. But one lesson is worth stating plainly: Some employees need more protection simply because they hold more power, more access, and more sensitive information. That starts with the C-suite, but it also applies to executive assistants, finance leaders, admins, and anyone else with privileged access.

Executives are high-value targets because they combine authority, visibility, and convenience-driven work habits. They approve payments, access sensitive strategy, and often log in from airports, hotels, and personal devices. That makes them especially attractive for phishing, impersonation, business email compromise, deepfake scams, and data theft. The right response is not to make life easier for them. It's to add smart friction in the places that matter most.

A strong executive protection program should include:

Phishing-resistant MFA, ideally hardware-based rather than SMS codes

Just-in-time privileged access instead of standing elevated permissions

Dedicated, locked-down devices for sensitive work

Stronger email and DLP controls to catch unusual forwarding, sharing, or exfiltration patterns

Focused coaching for executives and their inner circle, including assistants and chiefs of staff

Guidance for family and home networks, because executive risk doesn't stop at the office

Organizations can focus in on "white-glove" security, which means tighter controls, better support, and faster escalation when something looks off. If a control feels mildly annoying, that may be a sign it is doing its job.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Arielle Waldman, Features Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

These design tricks train people to click quickly, surrender data reflexively, and ignore warning signs. Over time, that weakens judgment. Employees who get used to manipulative prompts may be less likely to notice when a request is truly malicious — whether that’s a fake consent banner, a spoofed login page, a bogus app permission screen, or a prompt asking for sensitive information. Dark patterns blur the line between annoying and dangerous.

Another good rule: If you didn't sign up for a tool, don't create an account just because an email nudges you to. Unapproved signups can create shadow accounts that IT and security teams can't monitor or secure.

Finally, build a reporting culture around anything that feels off — surprise charges, mystery accounts, unusual permissions, or suspicious prompts. The more comfortable employees are raising small concerns, the easier it is to catch bigger issues before they spread.

Everyone knows password hygiene remains a challenge for most businesses, but risk in the login journey increasingly extends to the other seams around identity — the moments where users, devices, sessions, and recovery workflows intersect.

The threats include quishing, where a user scans a QR code from an email, webpage, or physical sign and lands on a convincing but malicious login screen. There's also push fatigue, where attackers bombard a user with approval requests until one gets accepted. And it includes session hijacking and token theft, where the attacker skips the password entirely and hops into an already authenticated session. Add SIM swapping to intercept SMS-based recovery, and the modern login chain starts to look brittle in several different places.

The long-term fix is to move toward phishing-resistant authentication, including FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, backed by enterprise controls that verify context, not just credentials. That means checking device posture, monitoring session behavior, requiring managed devices for sensitive systems, and reauthenticating when risk changes. In short: Don't just trust the login — trust the device, the session, and the user behavior behind it.

However, if this kind of full passkey rollout is not on the docket yet, there are practical steps organizations can take now to reduce login risk:

Turn on number matching for push-based MFA

Reduce or eliminate SMS-based authentication where possible

Shorten session lifetimes for high-risk apps

Require managed-device access for sensitive systems

Trigger reauthentication when device posture changes

And meanwhile, employee training should focus on a few clear habits: Don't scan login QR codes from unsolicited messages or unverified sources, for one, and never approve an unexpected SMS verification push.

To prevent session hijacking, log out of accounts when you finish using them, rather than just closing the browser tab. And avoid public Wi-Fi when you're doing sensitive things.

And finally, on the SIM-swapping front, switch from SMS MFA to Authenticator Apps that can't be intercepted via a phone network. You can also request that account changes require physical ID in-store or multilayered, out-of-band authentication before processing SIM changes.

Account takeover attacks are a bugbear that is unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but increasing friction and cost for attackers throughout the login process can really help and, hopefully, get you out of the low-hanging-fruit category at the very least.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Rob Wright, Senior News Director at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

Fall youth sports season means many parent-professionals are working from the sidelines — at soccer fields, hockey rinks, football stadiums, and school gyms — often on whatever free Wi-Fi happens to be available. That may not sound as risky as logging on at a major airport or hotel, but it still creates an opportunity for mistakes that attackers, pranksters, or opportunistic snoops can exploit.

Sophisticated nation-state actors are probably not camping out at your local rink. But there's still considerable risk if you connect to the wrong network. A hotspot with a name that closely resembles the venue's legitimate Wi-Fi can be enough to trick a busy parent checking email between periods or joining a meeting from the bleachers. Even a spoofed network set up as a joke can expose traffic, credentials, or session data if employees are careless.

Business readers that want to avoid their employer's penalty box should treat public connectivity anywhere as untrusted by default. Before joining a network, verify the exact Wi-Fi name with venue staff or posted signage. Disable auto-join so your device does not connect to similarly named networks without your knowledge. Use only approved secure remote access tools, keep endpoint protections enabled, and avoid handling sensitive work such as admin access, financial approvals, or password resets over public Wi-Fi unless it is absolutely necessary.

If you need connectivity, a personal hotspot is often the safer option — but only if it is configured properly. Use a strong password, change the default network name if it reveals your identity, and make sure the hotspot is not left open to nearby devices.

The broader lesson for Cybersecurity Awareness Month: Low-profile locations can still produce real security failures. The setting may feel routine, but the network risk is not.

Watch the video on this cybersecurity awareness tip from Alex Culafi, Senior News Writer at Dark Reading, on LinkedIn.

SEO poisoning turns a routine Google search into an attack path. Threat actors either build lookalike websites or compromise legitimate ones, then manipulate content and code so those pages rank highly in search results. The idea is that a user searching for software, a login page, or a partner site might simply click the top result, which happens to be poisoned, and subsequently hand over credentials or download malware.

Guidance on spotting fake websites specifically warns that SEO poisoning can push malicious sites to the top of search results, and Trend Micro’s 2026 research on more than 35,000 fake World Cup-related sites shows how easily attackers can industrialize fake-site campaigns around high-interest topics.

For business users, the safest habit is to stop trusting search rankings as a signal of legitimacy. Before clicking, inspect the URL for misspellings, extra words, odd country codes, or brand names that look slightly off. After clicking, be suspicious if the page immediately pushes a download, asks for credentials too early, triggers repeated redirects, throws pop-ups, or trips a browser warning. Those are strong signs that something is wrong.

Organizations should reinforce a few simple rules in awareness training:

Use bookmarks or manually typed URLs for key business apps, vendors, and partner portals.

Verify domains before downloading software or entering credentials.

Treat urgent install prompts and so-called ClickFix instructions as red flags.

Report suspicious search results, spoofed pages, and accidental downloads to IT immediately.

Isolate the device and change credentials quickly if a user may have interacted with a fake site.

The practical message for Cybersecurity Awareness Month: Search is a convenience layer, not a trust layer. Employees don't need to become threat hunters, but they do need to slow down long enough to verify where a search result is actually taking them. That pause can prevent a compromise.

#9867. FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm

Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”

The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”

Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

This entry was posted on Friday 9th of October 2026 08:17 PM

Arresting the *founder* rather than the negotiation firm itself is the detail that should worry operators the most. Individual accountability for running a negotiation service is essentially untested — the practice is legal in most jurisdictions as long as the customer is the victim of the incident rather than the perpetrator, and there’s no licensing or registration regime for it.

That gap means an arrest is a signal, not a fix. Expect more of these services to move offshore or rebrand under new ownership, and expect the tooling that makes them profitable (leak-site monitoring, initial-access-broker contact lists, automated follow-up) to keep scaling regardless of who gets charged.

The part I don’t see covered: how much of the value in this business is the *list* rather than the negotiation. If the negotiation contact itself is worth little to a criminal group — the customer already knows they’re breached — then arresting the negotiator mostly removes a service fee, not a capability. The durable asset is the broker/leak-site relationship feeding targets in.

What this arrest will do regardless is chill the negotiation industry: firms will start asking counsel to review every engagement letter, and some will quietly exit the business. One practical takeaway for defenders: this is another reminder to treat your IR retainer and negotiation playbooks as legal-adjacent documents. Get your outside counsel involved in the ransomware response plan before you need it, not after the FBI shows up with questions about who said what on your behalf.

Worth adding to the discussion of the FBI negotiation-company arrests: the practical gap most defenders have is not awareness of ShinyHunters, it is visibility into what the group actually does to get in.

Across the intrusions we have analyzed, the initial-access and exfiltration chain is unusually consistent and entirely built on commodity tooling:

– Remote access and support tools installed as a foothold (ScreenConnect, Screenovate, AnyDesk, Rclone) rather than exploiting a novel vulnerability. – Multi-week dwell times, so presence-based detection rarely triggers early. – Data staged out in chunks sized to stay under typical DLP alerting thresholds — a full customer or employee dataset rarely needs to leave in one transfer to be useful to the extortion side.

The practical consequence is that alerting on named malware is largely beside the point for this group; alerting on the *tools* and on small repetitive outbound flows is what actually catches the chain.

#9866. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

#9865. Why Your LLM Keeps Matching the Wrong Products (And Why a Better Prompt Won't Fix It)

CEO of Businessware Technologies, machine learning engineer

CEO of Businessware Technologies, machine learning engineer

CEO of Businessware Technologies, machine learning engineer

Imagine you have two product catalogs. One contains 10,000 items, the other 50,000. Your task is to find matching products, even though suppliers use different names, abbreviations, and formats.

Sounds like a perfect job for an LLM, right?

Modern language models understand context, recognize synonyms, and handle unstructured text pretty well. Just give the model two lists, ask it to find matching items, and you're done.

An LLM can understand both product names correctly and still return the wrong match.

The reason is simple: similar product names, identical products, and commercially acceptable substitutes are three different things.

While working on automated data matching problems, we've encountered several challenges that can't be solved simply by switching to a more powerful model or writing a better prompt.

Let's look at what goes wrong and how to build a more reliable matching process.

The lexical similarity is high. Most words overlap, the volume is the same, and both products are apple-based drinks.

But they're not identical products. One is juice with no added sugar, while the other is a sweetened juice drink.

If we're looking for an exact product match, this pair should be rejected.

The names look different, but EVOO is a common abbreviation for Extra Virgin Olive Oil, and the volumes are equivalent once normalized.

If the other relevant attributes match, this pair could be a valid match.

These are simplified examples, but they illustrate a fundamental problem.

An algorithm can be very good at measuring textual similarity without understanding whether two products are actually equivalent.

That requires looking at product attributes and the requirements of the matching task.

And sometimes the business doesn't need an identical product at all. It needs an acceptable substitute.

In that case, two products may have different brands or some different attributes and still be considered a valid match.

Should these products be considered a match?

We know it's coffee, and we know the package weight. But that's hardly enough to match it confidently with a specific product in another catalog.

We don't know the manufacturer, roast level, coffee variety, or other potentially important characteristics.

A human working with the catalog might open the supplier's product page, look up the missing information, and then make a decision.

An LLM that only receives the original product name doesn't have that information.

It might guess the missing attributes based on its general knowledge. But a guess is not the same as verified product data.

This matters when matching results are used for purchasing, price comparisons, or updating ERP records.

A wrong match can lead to a wrong order, an invalid price comparison, or incorrect data in a business system.

That's why it's worth checking whether the available information is sufficient before trying to make a matching decision.

If an important attribute is missing, the system may need to retrieve additional information, consult an external source, or send the case for human review.

Not every AI error can be fixed with better AI. Sometimes the system simply needs more data.

The most obvious way to automate product matching is to give an LLM two lists and ask it to return matching pairs.

This can work for small datasets, especially when product names are clear and contain enough information.

But things get complicated as catalogs grow.

First, the model has to do several jobs at once: find potential candidates, interpret product attributes, and decide which products match.

Second, processing costs increase. Sending large catalogs into the model's context for every request is expensive and often impractical.

Suppose the model returns the wrong product. What exactly went wrong?

Did it misunderstand an abbreviation? Miss an important attribute? Fail to consider the correct candidate? Or apply the wrong matching rule?

When everything happens inside one prompt, answering those questions isn't easy.

That's why we find it more practical to split large-scale catalog matching into several specialized steps.

Conventional algorithms can handle text cleaning and normalization. Lexical and semantic search can identify potential matches. An LLM can interpret ambiguous names and extract product attributes.

Final matching decisions can then be based on structured features, business rules, and a separate ranking algorithm.

There's no reason to use an LLM for every operation when a simpler method can do the job reliably and at a lower cost.

Let's look at a general approach that can be used when designing a product matching system.

Instead of comparing every product against every other product using an LLM, we can first narrow down the search space.

A common approach is to combine lexical and semantic similarity.

Lexical search works well for similar words, product codes, and naming conventions.

Semantic search helps find items with related meanings, even when their wording differs.

But there's an important limitation: if the correct product doesn't make it into the candidate list, the next stages won't be able to select it.

That's why candidate retrieval quality should be evaluated separately from final ranking quality.

Some systems need a short list of the most likely matches. Others need to find as many acceptable alternatives as possible.

These are different requirements, and they call for different retrieval strategies.

Once we have a set of candidates, we can extract and normalize the attributes needed for matching.

For food products, these might include product type, ingredients, weight, and packaging.

For electronic components, the important attributes could be manufacturer, model, technical specifications, and compatibility.

LLMs are particularly useful here because they can interpret unstructured names that are difficult to process with regular expressions or dictionaries alone.

But extracting the attributes is only half the job.

In one product category, a different manufacturer may be unacceptable. In another, products from different brands may be perfectly valid substitutes.

That's why simply checking whether every attribute matches is often not enough.

After extracting and comparing attributes, we can build a feature set for each product pair.

These features might include lexical similarity, semantic similarity, manufacturer agreement, matching attributes, and other signals.

A separate classifier or rule-based system can then evaluate how well the pair meets the matching requirements.

This way, the LLM doesn't have to handle every part of the decision-making process.

It also becomes possible to evaluate retrieval, attribute extraction, and ranking independently.

And that's especially useful when something goes wrong.

Instead of trying to fix the entire system by rewriting one prompt, we can investigate the specific component responsible for the error.

Even with a well-designed matching process, there's another challenge: product catalogs never stop changing.

Suppliers introduce new abbreviations. New brands appear. Product attributes and matching requirements evolve.

One way to adapt is to collect new examples and periodically fine-tune the model.

That makes sense when we actually need to change the model's learned behavior.

But if the change is simply a new synonym or business rule, fine-tuning may be unnecessary.

Suppose a company decides that products from different manufacturers can be considered equivalent in a particular category, as long as certain attributes match.

It's easier to store that rule in configuration than to teach an LLM to reproduce it through another training cycle.

But what about unusual matching cases that can't be described by one simple rule?

This is where retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, can help.

When a specialist validates a difficult product pair, that decision can be stored in a database of verified examples.

The next time a similar case appears, the system can retrieve the relevant historical example and provide it to the LLM as additional context.

This gives us two ways to manage changing knowledge:

It doesn't mean we'll never need fine-tuning again. But new data doesn't always have to mean changing model weights.

Sometimes updating a dictionary, a configuration rule, or a set of validated examples is enough.

Of course, RAG needs its own quality controls. An outdated or irrelevant example can lead to the wrong decision, too.

Let's say your matching system keeps making mistakes with a certain group of products.

The first instinct might be to improve the prompt or switch to a more powerful LLM.

Before doing that, it's worth checking a few things.

1. Was the correct product in the candidate list?

If the correct item never appeared in the search results, the final model had no chance of selecting it.

The problem may be in lexical or semantic retrieval, not ranking.

2. Was there enough information in the input data?

If the original product name doesn't include important attributes, the model may not have enough evidence to make a confident decision.

Data enrichment or human review may help more than another prompt.

3. Were the attributes extracted and normalized correctly?

Even if the LLM identified the attributes correctly, the next component might compare their values incorrectly.

Equivalent units or alternative names may be treated as conflicts.

4. Were the right business rules applied?

The same attribute can have different importance across product categories.

If the system applies a universal rule where a category-specific rule is needed, the problem may be in the matching logic rather than the LLM.

5. Is it actually a model capability problem?

If retrieval, input data, attributes, and rules all look correct, then it's worth examining the model itself.

Maybe it struggles to interpret certain terminology or follow the required instructions.

At that point, changing the prompt, providing additional context, trying another model, or fine-tuning may be reasonable options.

These checks won't solve every matching problem, but they help identify where the error starts before spending time and money changing the entire system.

Splitting matching into several stages makes the system easier to control, but it also adds complexity.

And cloud LLM calls come with recurring costs.

One option is to extract detailed attributes for every product in the entire catalog before matching begins.

This could help find acceptable substitutes with very different names.

But processing hundreds of thousands of products this way can get expensive.

An alternative is to use relatively cheap candidate retrieval first and apply the LLM only to the selected products.

That reduces costs but introduces the risk of missing valid matches at the first stage.

So there's a trade-off between recall, processing speed, and cost.

For some businesses, missing a valid match can be a costly mistake. For others, sending a small number of difficult cases for human review may be perfectly acceptable.

The same reasoning applies when choosing between cloud and local models.

Local inference may be cheaper at high and stable processing volumes, but it requires infrastructure, maintenance, and, when fine-tuning is involved, ongoing work with training data.

Cloud models reduce the need for some of that infrastructure but introduce usage-based costs.

That's why the comparison shouldn't be limited to the price of an API call.

What matters is the total cost of producing results at the required quality level.

When an LLM matches two products incorrectly, the natural reaction is to improve the prompt, choose a more powerful model, or prepare a new dataset for fine-tuning.

But before changing the model, it's worth understanding why the mistake happened.

Maybe the correct candidate never appeared in the search results. Maybe an important attribute was missing from the input data. Or maybe two equivalent values were incorrectly treated as conflicting.

Sometimes the system simply doesn't know the business rule that determines whether two products should be considered a match.

These problems require different solutions.

Reliable product catalog matching depends on more than the language model's capabilities. It also depends on data quality, candidate retrieval, structured attributes, and matching rules.

Instead of trying to teach one model everything, it's often more practical to build a system where each component does its own job and changing knowledge can be updated without rebuilding the entire architecture.

Your Logistics Documents Are Eating Your Margins. Here’s How to Calculate the Damage

#9864. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎

#9863. Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:

<|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason,

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:

Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command:

You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID:

The repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model).

You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more.

llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K.

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:

The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API:

The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content.

The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs.

After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server:

This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request using the same Hub model ID:

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:

This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.
