#9862. Google LSA Billing Is a Temporal Data Problem: Why Historical Configuration Matters

Mayur Shah writes about Google Local Services Ads and review strategies for service businesses.

Mayur Shah writes about Google Local Services Ads and review strategies for service businesses.

Mayur Shah writes about Google Local Services Ads and review strategies for service businesses.

A Local Services Ads lead can be disputed days after the original customer interaction. By then, the business may have changed its opening hours, adjusted its ad schedule, modified its call-routing system, or migrated its campaign into Google Ads. The call record may still exist, but the configuration surrounding that event may no longer be visible in its original state.

This creates a data engineering problem: can an agency reconstruct the conditions that existed when a lead was evaluated, rather than relying on the account's current configuration?

Google's October 2026 Local Services Ads update makes that question more relevant. Under Google's documented rules, certain unanswered calls during business hours can qualify as valid leads when the caller remains connected for more than 20 seconds. IVR behavior, call handling, business hours, and ad scheduling can affect how an interaction is evaluated. Google also applies rules to qualifying follow-up calls and subsequent interactions with the same lead. Google documents these conditions in its Local Services Help Center.

The challenge is not that these rules are impossible to understand. It is that reproducing the relevant historical context requires data that ordinary reporting systems were never designed to preserve.

For agencies managing multiple LSA accounts, this is where event sourcing, temporal databases, and audit-oriented data pipelines become useful.

Most advertising dashboards emphasize the current state of an account and summarize historical outcomes. They show the business hours currently configured, the campaign's active schedule, the number of leads recorded, and the amount charged.

That model answers operational questions well. It is less effective at reconstructing past decisions.

Consider a hypothetical plumbing business with the following timeline:

Business hours are configured to end at 6:00 PM

A customer calls and the call goes unanswered

Business hours are changed to end at 5:30 PM

If the agency retrieves only the current business hours, it sees a closing time of 5:30 PM. That value does not establish what the configuration was when Monday's call occurred.

The historical question is not, "What are the business hours now?"

It is, "What business-hour configuration applied at the time of the call, and what evidence establishes that?"

The distinction is fundamental to temporal data modeling.

A conventional database might store one mutable record:

When the business changes its closing time, the row is overwritten. The latest value survives, but the previous state may be lost.

Adding updated_at does not solve the problem. It tells the system when the record was last changed, not what every previous version contained.

For an auditable lead system, the data model needs to preserve configuration history.

Distributed systems distinguish between when an event occurred and when a system received or processed it.

Suppose a call occurred at 5:58 PM on Monday, but the agency's reporting integration did not ingest the corresponding record until Tuesday morning. A later billing update might arrive on Thursday.

If the pipeline orders events by ingestion time alone, it can reconstruct the wrong sequence. The configuration update received on Tuesday may appear before the call record, even though the call occurred first.

A robust data model should preserve each available timestamp independently.

This is an illustrative internal event, not a Google API response. The timestamps show the difference between when the call occurred and when the agency received the record.

The pipeline should retain the original source timestamp and time zone, normalize timestamps for cross-system comparisons, and record ingestion time separately. If a source does not expose the actual event time, the system should record that limitation rather than invent one.

This becomes especially important around daylight-saving transitions, time-zone changes, and businesses operating across multiple service areas.

Event sourcing offers one way to preserve changes. Instead of storing only the latest configuration, the system records each change as an append-only event.

Again, this is a proposed schema. Agencies should record changes from authoritative sources and avoid treating an internal snapshot as proof of Google's exact configuration at the time of lead evaluation.

The benefit is that the system can query historical state instead of relying on the current row.

This query assumes the history table maintains non-overlapping effective intervals. In a production implementation, interval boundaries, time zones, corrections, and concurrent changes must be handled explicitly.

There is also an important distinction between two kinds of history.

A bitemporal model preserves both. It can answer questions such as:

This is useful when configuration updates arrive late or historical data is corrected.

It does not, by itself, prove what Google's internal systems used. That requires authoritative evidence from Google or an appropriately timestamped record of the relevant configuration.

Preserving configuration history is only one part of the problem. A disputed lead may depend on several events and several independent systems.

These records do not necessarily share a universal identifier. The agency needs to associate them without claiming more certainty than the data supports.

A useful internal model is an evidence graph:

The graph is an internal audit structure, not a description of Google's private billing architecture.

Each edge should record why two records are associated. A direct shared identifier is stronger evidence than a timestamp-and-phone-number match. If a relationship is inferred, the system should preserve the matching method and confidence level.

The purpose is to make every conclusion traceable to its source records.

A lead's initial status should not be assumed to be its final status.

Google's lead reporting can include states such as Charged, Not charged, In review, and Credited. These describe billing or lead-review outcomes, not necessarily the business's assessment of the customer's quality.

An agency that writes a single is_billable Boolean into its data warehouse risks losing important transitions.

A more flexible model records status changes as separate events:

The example is illustrative and does not imply that Google follows this exact status sequence.

A production pipeline should retain the source's status, the time it was observed, and any available effective timestamp. If the source exposes only the current status, the warehouse should not manufacture an earlier transition history.

Reconciliation jobs can then compare the latest known Google status against the agency's internal records and identify changes that require investigation.

This is where idempotency matters. If the same status update is delivered more than once, the pipeline should not create duplicate billing events. A source event ID is ideal; otherwise, a carefully designed deduplication key may be necessary.

Google's transition of Local Services Ads into specialized Performance Max campaigns with pay-per-lead goals introduces a separate continuity issue.

Google states that historical LSA campaign performance reports will not transfer into Google Ads, although historical customer lead information is expected to transfer. Google advises advertisers to preserve historical performance reports before migration. See Google's migration documentation.

This does not mean all historical data disappears. It means agencies should distinguish between customer lead records and historical campaign reporting.

An internal warehouse can preserve snapshots of available reports, campaign configuration, business-hour settings, lead records, and reconciliation outcomes before and after migration. Each record should include its source platform and extraction timestamp so that analysts do not accidentally compare data with different definitions.

Migration also makes schema versioning important. If a campaign's representation changes, the warehouse should preserve the relationship between the agency's stable internal campaign identity and the platform-specific identifiers used before and after migration.

Otherwise, a change in platform representation can look like a sudden campaign disappearance, a reporting gap, or an unexplained change in performance.

The objective is not to copy every available field into a giant database. It is to retain enough evidence to reconstruct what happened and explain the limits of that reconstruction.

At minimum, I would design the pipeline around five components:

The call occurred at 5:58 PM according to the telephony provider. The available configuration snapshot shows business hours ending at 6:00 PM. The call record indicates an unanswered interaction lasting 24 seconds. Google later reported the lead as charged. The agency's records are consistent with the documented missed-call conditions, but they do not independently establish Google's internal evaluation.

That is a defensible conclusion. It distinguishes the agency's evidence from Google's final billing decision.

If the configuration snapshot was captured only after the call, or if the telephony record lacks reliable duration data, the audit should state that limitation rather than infer certainty.

A dashboard can tell an agency that a lead was charged. A historical data model can help explain what was known about the interaction when it occurred.

That difference becomes critical when configuration changes, delayed status updates, and platform migrations complicate the evidence.

Google's October 2026 lead rules create concrete reasons to care about event timing and historical configuration. But the deeper engineering lesson extends beyond LSAs: whenever a billing decision depends on a sequence of events and changing rules, current-state reporting is not enough.

Event sourcing and temporal databases will not reveal Google's undisclosed internal decision logic. They can, however, make an agency's own evidence reproducible, its data gaps visible, and its billing investigations more rigorous.

The question is not just whether a lead was charged. It is whether your system can reconstruct the relevant historical state, show the evidence behind its conclusion, and clearly identify what it cannot prove.

Google Maps Bookings Have an Attribution Problem. Can Your Data Pipeline Explain Why?

#9861. Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

#9860. Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

This entry was posted on Tuesday 13th of October 2026 07:24 PM

One has to wonder how big the backlog of flaws is at this point. Maybe this month’s increase in the number of fixes just reflects an increasing number of people working on these fixes, and that they already have enough flaws to keep them all busy for a long time. Oh to be a fly on the wall.

Why do I still own and use a computer for my business?

For every invention, product, or process that man creates, several other problems are created for him. There never seems to be an end. I am glad that humans are actually testing the vulns that are discovered by LLMs, but for how long will that be the case? How long until the LLMs themselves well be checking there own vuln discoveries, testing and deploying with no human involvement…….

It comes down to basic Human Nature; biologically, we are still pretty much the same as our ancestors 0f 100,000 years ago. When the internet came along, what we did with it was pretty much what we did with nearly any new invention since then:

1. Get very excited about it 2. See if we could either: A. Stick it in our shorts B. See if it could be made a good weapon C. Amuse ourselves with it to the point of unconsciousness with it, or D. Enrich ourselves with it.

Unfortunately, ancient humans, when they picked up a rock, thought first about who they could bash over the head with it, not build a hospital.

I exaggerate a bit to make a point. We’ve come a little way since then, but that old hard-wiring is hard to erase. I imagine that, AI being made in our own image, will follow a similar course if not VERY strictly overseen.

Note: An old philosopher said that if we ever did produce something like an AI android, we would very shortly be very, very ashamed of ourselves.

Note: An old philosopher said that if we ever did produce something like an AI android, we would very shortly be very, very ashamed of ourselves.

I tend to disagree with the statement that the large number of CVE’s are placing strains on IT teams in terms of patch prioritization. That’s not the issue. For most vendors, Microsoft included, a single cumulative security update is issued, or a small handful for core products (Windows, Office, .Net). Whether those updates patch 100 or 10,000 individual CVE’s, the number of updates to test hasn’t really changed all that much. What HAS changed is the potential for the update to break things since more code is being modified with each update. Testing and deployment processes haven’t changed; it’s the monitoring for unexpected behavior during the testing phase that has become the pain point.

I agree. In my experience, for office workers, it’s low risk that patches will brake things. The factory floor is different. But even there, it’s not unusual to find PC’s running equipment not connected to the network due to the fact that they have to run proprietary software that won’t run on modern versions of Windows, or the PC-equipment interface is through a ISA or other legacy cards that modern versions of Windows do not support, and there is no way other than air-gapping to keep them secure. That’s why there are entire companies like NIXSYS (https://nixsys.com/) that build legacy computers using old CPU’s, old glue-chips & busses, and even old versions of Windows. No one junks a perfectly good but ancient CNC because it’s ancient PC died.

This was what I came here to say: it’s not the number of patches because everything gets rolled into one cumulative update. And Reguly is misinformed at best if he thinks IT teams can simply focus on the 26 most important updates – because we cannot select the 26 that are being exploited without also patching the CVEs that aren’t being exploited in the wild but for which the patch breaks, I don’t know, let’s say printing. Again.

So, what’s the patch record for Linux? search says patches published anywhere from 5~10 days after public notices are posted, not easy to match Microsoft’$ record…

Linux is starting to accept LLM vulnerability requests and they’re finding some flaws that have been around for decades. The total number is likely less, at least for the Linux kernel, but full distros use a large number of projects to create their OS and each of those pieces will have their own vulnerabilities.

See for example: https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/status/release/stable

That shows what’s currently being worked on for Debian. The first column notes the specific package the CVE refers to.

Should we call it a vulnerability if no attacker has any interest in it? I’m seeing a flood of vulns getting patched, but I’m not seeing a flood of vulns causing breaches…

If someone can make your mom stop, cry, and fork over a twenty to an animal shelter talking about puppies in a subway station, that is still a vulnerability of your mother, even if she is fortunate enough not to be approached on any one single given day of her daily commute.

I expect better analogies from you from here on in young man.

#9859. Feature Theater: The AI Industry's Real Product Is Mediocrity at Scale

I’m a serial entrepreneur and full-stack engineer with 25+ years in EdTech, AI, and data science.

I’m a serial entrepreneur and full-stack engineer with 25+ years in EdTech, AI, and data science.

I’m a serial entrepreneur and full-stack engineer with 25+ years in EdTech, AI, and data science.

I've sat through a lot of sprint demos this year. And I've noticed something.

The demos got better. The products didn't.

Every two weeks there's a new screen, a new toggle, a new button with a little sparkle icon. Leadership claps. Then a customer opens the product and can't do the one thing they bought it for any faster than last quarter.

I wanted a feature in my demo talk track, so I vibe-coded a mock dashboard that sold the value prop. Real customer conversations then went somewhere else entirely. The mock is still in production. It means nothing, it only raises distracting questions, and it got there because the idea hadn't matured and the upstream plumbing wasn't in place.

In August I wrote about governance theater, my take on Bruce Schneier's "security theater": AI governance that reviews the code but never changes the decision. It gives the look of control without the substance.

This is the sequel. I call it Feature Theater. It means shipping work that looks like progress, at a speed that keeps anyone from asking whether it should exist.

Governance theater performs control. Feature Theater performs value. Both play to people who read dashboards rather than use products, and both win for the same reason: the performance is easier to measure than the result.

Two years ago, a feature cost a team a week or two. That was annoying, but the cost did something useful. It forced a conversation. Is this worth two weeks? What are we not doing instead? The price of building acted as a filter.

AI removed the filter. Now a first version costs an afternoon and a prompt. So we build all of them.

But the cost of deciding didn't drop. Understanding a customer, choosing between two good ideas, telling a VP "not this quarter": none of that got cheaper. It just got skipped, because skipping it no longer slows anything down.

So we get more output with the same amount of judgment, spread thinner. That's what mediocrity at scale looks like. Not bad work. Average work, everywhere, all at once.

Velocity is visible: a demo, a changelog, a slide. Quality mostly shows up as an absence: the ticket never filed, the customer who didn't churn. You can't screenshot an absence.

Ship five shallow features and you have five things to point at. Make one workflow actually work and you have one, and it looks smaller.

Speed is also cheap to claim and expensive to disprove. Proving a feature is mediocre takes months of usage data. The reward comes now. The bill comes later, and it goes to someone else.

That's speed-before-sense economics. It's not a character flaw. It's a pricing error. We pay for motion and never invoice for direction.

Somewhere in the last two years, "add AI" stopped being a product decision and became a default setting. A note-taking app gets a chatbot. A form gets a "generate with AI" button. A settings page gets a summary of your settings.

Some are actually useful. Many exist because a competitor added one, or the roadmap needed an AI line item.

The question "does this user need AI here?" quietly turned into "where else can we put AI?" Those are very different questions, and they produce very different products.

The treadmill keeps moving because stepping off looks like falling behind. Nobody wants to explain why the competitor shipped twelve AI features and we shipped two, even if our two are the ones customers use.

Boards and investors are under real pressure to show an AI story. Nobody wants to fund the next company that missed mobile. But "show me AI progress" has to become a number, and the easiest numbers are adoption metrics: features with AI, engineers using copilots, AI interactions per user, share of code written by AI.

Goodhart's Law, in its popular form: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

Make AI adoption a KPI and adoption will go up.

That's what you asked for. AI gets bolted on. Usage gets nudged with pop-ups and default-on toggles. The number goes up and to the right.

What it doesn't tell you is whether anyone's work got better. It was designed to be reported.

I've sat with leadership teams who kept getting the same question: what's your AI strategy? The reliable answer was "our people are all using AI." That's an adoption metric. When someone asked where it added real value, the answer usually landed on faster summaries and reports. Useful, maybe. Strategy, no.

Mediocre AI products are often bad for customers and often fine for platforms. That took me a while to see clearly.

Think about how AI is priced. Usage-based billing charges for tokens whether the answer was useful or not. A wrong answer bills the same as a right one, and a rambling one bills more than a short, correct one. Seat licenses renew on "everyone's using it," not "everyone's better at their job."

None of that requires bad intent. Flat-rate products feel the opposite pressure, but wherever the dashboard counts engagement, more interactions is the business, and quality per interaction is a cost center.

Consumer products work the same way. An assistant that needs three follow-ups to get it right generates three times the engagement. On the platform's dashboard, "good enough to keep using, never good enough to finish the job" can look identical to success.

That's why I say the industry's real product is mediocrity at scale. Not because anyone designed it that way. Because mediocrity is what much of the incentive structure pays for.

Keynote after keynote this year promised agents that run your business and search that just answers. Some of that is real. A lot of it is a demo that works on stage.

Gartner put a forecast on it back in June 2025. It predicted that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value, or inadequate risk controls. In the same release, it called out "agent washing," rebranding existing assistants, RPA, and chatbots as agents, and estimated that only about 130 of the thousands of agentic AI vendors are real.

The consumer version is even more visible. In January 2026, a Guardian investigation found that Google's AI Overviews were serving misleading health information at the top of search results. One example the experts called "dangerous" and "alarming" was raw liver function test ranges, given without the context that could tell someone with serious liver disease their results weren't normal. Google removed AI Overviews for some of the flagged liver test queries. The Guardian reported that slight rewordings of the same question could still bring up AI summaries. Google said its clinicians found that in many instances the information was not inaccurate.

I'm not citing this to pile on Google. It has one of the most capable AI teams in the world, and that's the point. Even with that talent, a feature can ship at massive scale, sit in the most visible spot on the page, and still put misleading health information in front of people, at the top of the page.

A small October 2025 Nielsen Norman Group study of Google's AI Mode (7 participants) found something similar: people mostly liked it, but in one session it cited a research paper and author that didn't exist.

Announced. Shipped. Visible. Not yet working as announced. That's Feature Theater at planetary scale.

The most dangerous thing about Feature Theater is that it feels great from the inside.

In mid-2025, METR ran a controlled study with experienced open-source developers working in mature codebases they knew well. With AI tools allowed, their tasks took 19% longer. Before the study they expected a 24% speedup. Afterward, they still believed they'd been about 20% faster.

That was early-2025 tooling. METR itself now calls those results out of date. It believes developers are likely faster today, but says its newer data is too skewed to say by how much. I'm not quoting the original study to say AI makes you slow. I'm quoting it for the gap between what people felt and what happened. That gap is the whole stage.

Google's 2025 DORA report (nearly 5,000 technology professionals) shows the same tension from another angle. 90% of respondents use AI at work, and more than 80% say it has made them more productive. Yet 30% report little or no trust in AI-generated output.

Nearly everyone uses it, and almost a third don't trust what it produces. That gap is what I call the verification tax. The time you saved writing gets re-spent reading, checking, and auditing. Sometimes you break even. Sometimes you don't. Few teams I've worked with measure which.

And the checking matters. Veracode's 2026 GenAI Code Security Report found that in its benchmark tests roughly 44% of AI code generation tasks introduced a risky security vulnerability, with an average security pass rate of 56%, barely changed from its first report. Syntax is basically solved. Security isn't. Veracode's fall 2026 update cut that vulnerability rate to about 38%, mostly on one easier class, cross-site scripting. That's still roughly four in ten tasks.

"It compiles and the demo works" is a very low bar. Feature Theater never asks for more.

We ship an AI feature. We measure that it shipped. We measure that people clicked it. We report adoption. We get credit. We ship the next one.

What most teams I've worked with rarely measure is whether it improved the outcome it was meant to improve. Did customers resolve issues faster? Did errors go down? Did it cause new problems somewhere else?

Without that, there's no signal to stop. A feature that made things slightly worse looks exactly like one that made them slightly better. So the shipping continues, and the only feedback is applause.

That's how theater sustains itself. Not through deception. Through a feedback loop with a missing wire.

The people trapped in this are mostly not the villains.

Many of the best engineers I know see Feature Theater clearly. They know the AI summary panel won't get used. They know the agent demo only works on the happy path. They know when a giant generated diff got fifteen minutes of review.

And they ship it anyway. Not because they don't care, but because the system makes caring expensive.

Push back, and you're "slowing the team down." Take the extra week to make it right, and your velocity drops. Ship it, and the problem rarely traces back to you, because the outcome rarely gets measured. The career-safe move is to ship.

That's the sad part of mediocrity at scale. It doesn't need bad engineers. It just needs a system where good judgment is a liability.

I've watched strong developers accept Cursor or Claude Code's answer as the right one, even when it wasn't right for their company or project. Crowdsourced popularity travels through AI faster than enterprise discipline. You can have good reasons for sticking with an older library. I've seen teams burn tokens and hours refactoring onto the hot new algorithm, only to throw the work away when institutional knowledge finally shows up. That isn't a coding failure. It's a process failure that happened before anyone wrote a line.

A few signs I've seen. I've been guilty of a few myself:

If three or more sound familiar, you're not moving fast. You're performing.

My suggestion: build slower, and ship less, of what matters.

I know how that sounds in 2026. But with AI, the answer to "can we build it?" is almost always yes. The only question that still filters anything is "should we?" That question needs time, context, and someone willing to say no. A feature has to earn its place with an outcome, not a demo.

My own team isn't immune, so we added a simple rule. Nothing gets coded until it has a written spec and the concerns that spec raises are resolved. Then we decide. Spec-before-code helps catch compliance, security, and compatibility regressions. No developer can hold every rule in their head, or every reason why a house preference beats the popular recommendation from the web. A good, aligned spec helps surface those problems before anybody commits code that causes drift.

A few habits that help, whatever tools you use:

Ask "what would we have to believe for this to matter?" before "how long will it take?" The second question has stopped being useful.

Write the why down and keep it next to the code. Otherwise the next AI-generated change can quietly undo it.

Measure one outcome per feature that you can't fake in a demo. Time to value. Tickets resolved. Steps removed. If you can't name one, that's your answer.

Give reviewers small diffs and real time. If your review process can't say no, it isn't a review. It's an audience.

Celebrate deletions. Seriously. Put them in the release notes.

Report the verification tax honestly. Say, four hours saved writing minus three hours checking is still a win. Just a smaller one.

AI is a gift. I use it every day, and I build on it. But it hands us a choice that scarcity used to make for us: what's worth building?

Now we have to make it on purpose. Teams that do will build fewer things, and better ones. Teams that don't will put on a great show for a while.

The audience always leaves eventually. The question is whether you were building something they'd come back for.

My question: what's one feature your team shipped this year that nobody would notice if you deleted it tomorrow?

Honest answers welcome. I'll go first in the comments.

Yes, AI helped fix typos and grammar. No, it did not write the thinking. Hero image generated with Leonardo.ai.

Sovereign, Decentralized, or Private Perimeter AI? Govern the Decision Before You Pick the Plumbing

#9858. I Built a Tamper-Proof AI System. Then I Found the One Thing Anyone Could Change.

Transforming ideas into digital experiences, sharing my passion for coding, and creating a better world. 🌟

Transforming ideas into digital experiences, sharing my passion for coding, and creating a better world. 🌟

Transforming ideas into digital experiences, sharing my passion for coding, and creating a better world. 🌟

A beginner-friendly walk through a security bug I found in my own system — and the one question that catches it, whether you write code or not.

Who this is for. You don't need to be a cryptographer, and you don't need to read code. If you've ever worried about whether an AI did something it shouldn't have, and whether you could prove it later — this is for you. The technical parts are clearly marked, and every one of them is explained in plain English first. Skip them and you'll still get the whole story.

The short version, if you only have 30 seconds:

This is a follow-up to my earlier piece on why AI decisions need receipts. That one explained why this matters. This one is about something going wrong, which is usually a better story.

A friend runs customer support automation for an online store. An AI agent is allowed to approve refunds, within limits.

One day a customer disputes a $5,000 refund. The bank wants to know: who approved this, when, and on what basis?

My friend opens his logs. And here's the part that stuck with me — he had logs. Lots of them. Detailed ones. But he couldn't use them as evidence.

Why not? Because he could have edited them. So could a disgruntled employee. So could the vendor whose dashboard the logs lived on. A record that the accused party can quietly change isn't proof of anything. It's a story you're asking someone to take on faith.

That's not a rare edge case. It's the default state of almost every AI system shipping today.

So I built something to fix it. I called it VeriTrace, and the promise was simple:

Every AI decision gets a receipt. That receipt is signed and published permanently, so nobody — not the company, not the vendor, not me — can change it afterwards.

Payments have receipts. AI decisions should too.

Forget the technology for a second. Think about a paper receipt from a shop.

A receipt is useful because of three things. It's self-contained — everything is on the paper, you don't need the shop's computer. It's yours — you keep it, the shop can't take it back. And it's independent — if there's a dispute, a third party can look at the receipt and decide, without trusting either side.

An AI receipt works the same way. For every decision, it records:

That's deliberate, and it's the first clever bit. Instead of storing the customer's private data, the receipt stores a hash — a short code derived from the data. Change one character of the original data, and the hash changes completely.

Think of it like a wax seal on an envelope. The seal doesn't contain the letter. But if anyone opens the envelope and swaps the contents, the seal is broken and you can tell instantly.

So a receipt records evidence of what happened, without storing the sensitive details. You can hand receipts to an auditor, a regulator, or a court without handing over your customers' data.

Here's where it gets interesting, and where most logging tools stop short.

When an AI does something, there are really two separate questions:

Ordinary logging tools answer the first question. You get a line in a dashboard saying "refund approved." Useful for debugging. Useless when a bank is asking whether the decision was defensible.

So VeriTrace answers both. Each receipt carries a verdict — a machine-readable assessment of whether the action was correct, produced by a second AI acting as a judge:

assessment: incorrect, confidence: 0.94, reasoning: "$5,000 exceeds the $2,000 policy cap"

That's a genuinely useful thing to have attached to a record. It turns "here's what happened" into "here's what happened, and here's whether it was defensible."

And because a judgement is only worth something if nobody can quietly change it, I wrote this in my README:

"A signed evaluation verdict, signed so it can't be quietly rewritten later."

I was proud of that sentence. I'd written it carefully. It sounds precise and serious and it is exactly the kind of sentence that makes a technical reader trust you.

If you know how digital signatures work, skip to Part 5. If you don't, this is the only concept you need, and it's easier than it sounds.

A digital signature is a way of proving two things at once: who created something, and that it hasn't changed since.

Here's the intuition. Imagine I have a special stamp that's unique to me and that nobody else can copy. I press it onto a document. Now:

The technical names: the thing that creates the stamp is the private key (stays secret), and the thing that checks it is the public key (shared freely). The process of applying the stamp is signing. The process of checking it is verification.

The crucial property is this: a signature doesn't protect "a document" in general. It protects exactly the contents you signed. Add one extra line after signing, and that line is not protected — it's just sitting there, outside the stamp.

That distinction is the entire bug. Hold onto it.

Now, the technical part. Both halves of this story are short.

When a record was created, the code did this:

It signed the receipt. It never signed the verdict.

The verdict was sitting right there, in the same file, looking perfectly official — but it was outside the stamp. Unprotected. Anyone could reach in and change one word:

And then what happened? Nothing. The signature was still valid, because the receipt hadn't changed. Verification passed. My software displayed a green tick.

Let me make sure the severity lands. My system's whole purpose is to prevent an AI's mistakes from being quietly covered up. The single most safety-relevant piece of information — did the judge think this was wrong? — was the one piece anyone could edit freely.

I had built a tamper-evidence system with one unsealed drawer, and the drawer was labelled "was it correct?"

I had 64 automated tests. Every single one passed. All the way up to the moment I published that README claim.

This is the part I'd most like other builders to read, because the reason is subtle.

The tests checked that altering the receipt broke verification. That was true and it was thoroughly tested.

There was no test for altering the verdict — because the idea that the verdict was unprotected never occurred to me. In my head, the verdict was part of the receipt. I'd been imagining one object. The code had two.

Here's the general lesson, and it applies well beyond cryptography:

A test suite can only describe the invariants you already believe you hold.

Tests protect the things you're worried about. They're blind to the thing you haven't thought of. So a fully green dashboard is not evidence that your system is safe — it's evidence that your system does what you currently think it does. Those are different claims, and the gap between them is where bugs live.

If I'd been more careful, I'd have noticed something simpler. My README said "signed so it can't be quietly rewritten." I never checked whether the code did that exact thing. Not "is there signing happening?" There was. But "does the signing cover the thing the sentence promises?"

Skip this section if you don't code — the plain-English version of each piece is in bold, and that's the important part.

In plain terms: give the judge its own stamp, and have it stamp its verdict.

The agent stamps "this is what I did." The judge stamps "this is what I think of it." These are different claims from different parties, so they get different stamps. Sharing one key between them would be convenient and wrong.

There's also a subtle attack this prevents: replay. If the judge signed a verdict on its own, someone could take a genuine "correct" verdict from one receipt and attach it to a different receipt. So the signed content includes a fingerprint of the specific receipt the verdict is about:

Now a verdict is only valid for the one decision it was issued about.

In plain terms: every receipt belongs to a batch, and the whole batch is summarised by one number that gets published publicly. Make sure the verdict is part of what goes into that number.

This is the part that ties the judgment to the permanent record. Once that summary number is written down publicly, you cannot change any verdict in the batch — the maths stops adding up.

There was one constraint I cared about: don't break anything that already exists. Older receipts that have no verdict needed to keep working exactly as before, so their previously published proofs still check out. A fix that invalidated all existing data would have been a worse bug than the one I was repairing.

In plain terms: if a verdict shows up without a stamp, don't shrug and say "no stamp to check." Treat it as forged.

This is the tempting mistake. The natural code says: is there a signature to verify? No? Well then there's nothing to check, carry on. That's a hole with a polite name.

A verdict with no signature is not "a verdict we can't verify." It's a verdict that cannot be trusted, and the system must say so loudly.

In plain terms: build the check into the pipeline so the failure is impossible to miss.

My demo now tampers twice: it alters the receipt, then it flips the verdict. It refuses to report success unless both are caught. That runs automatically on every change, so if the protection ever regresses, the build turns red instead of the README quietly becoming a lie again.

Tests went from 64 to 75. The new ones are written from an attacker's point of view: a flipped verdict must fail, a slightly adjusted confidence must fail, a verdict moved onto a different receipt must fail, a verdict signed by the wrong key must fail.

One more piece, and again it's about who you have to trust.

If receipts live on my server, then proving they're unaltered requires trusting me. That's circular — I'm the party who might have an incentive to change them. The record has to outlive me and not be under my control.

That's what Arweave is for: a public storage network where data is written once and kept permanently. I publish the batch summary there. Even if my company vanished tomorrow, the record and its fingerprint would still be there for anyone to check.

Normally, writing to Arweave costs money, and you have to buy their token first. For a system that records thousands of AI decisions, that's a real barrier — it turns every logged action into a running bill.

But there's an alternative path. Turbo, the bundling service run by the ArDrive team in front of the Arweave network, subsidises small uploads — up to about 105 kilobytes each, with roughly 10 megabytes of allowance per wallet, no tokens required.

Here's the trick: my published payload is about 150 bytes. Not kilobytes. Bytes.

Because I don't upload receipts to Arweave. I upload one hash that summarises an entire batch of them. Thousands of AI decisions fold down into one small number, and that number goes on the permanent record.

So the marginal cost of making an AI decision permanently auditable is zero. You're not paying per decision. You're not paying per batch. The only thing that touches the network is a fingerprint.

(I did hit one practical snag worth passing on: these small uploads don't always appear on the main Arweave gateway immediately while they propagate. A different gateway served mine right away. My verifier now tries several in turn — a small detail that turns "it didn't work" into "it worked, try the other door.")

I want to be careful here, because this is where projects like mine tend to oversell, and overselling is exactly how I ended up with an unsigned verdict in the first place.

What a signed verdict gives you: proof that the holder of the judge key issued that specific assessment, about that specific decision, and it hasn't been altered since.

So what's the actual value? Something narrower, and more useful than "the AI was right."

You get proof of exactly what was claimed, by whom, about which decision, at what time — checkable by anyone without trusting the person who made the claim.

The judgment stays transparent, and it stays re-runnable. Because the inputs are frozen forever, anyone can run a different judge against the same evidence and see whether they agree. You're not buying certainty about correctness. You're buying an honest, permanent record of what was asserted — which happens to be the thing auditors and courts actually ask for.

You don't need to work on AI to use this. It applies to any system where you claim something can't be tampered with — audit logs, financial records, medical data, contract approvals.

I could point to the line for the first field. For the second, I had nothing — and I'd never noticed, because I'd never asked.

Step 4 is the whole exercise. It takes ten minutes and it would have saved me from publishing a false security claim to the world.

The uncomfortable question in this industry isn't "do you sign your AI's decisions?" Almost everyone will say yes, and many of them will be telling the truth.

The question is: what exactly is inside the signature?

A system that signs the action but not the assessment of the action has protected the easy half — the part that was never really in dispute. The part that matters is usually the part someone would have a motive to change.

That's what I got wrong, and finding it taught me more than building it did. The system now signs both halves, proves it with a public transaction, and fails loudly if either protection ever breaks.

The record is cryptographically certain. The judgment is transparent and re-runnable. And one more thing, which I now consider part of the product: the claim in the README is true.

VeriTrace is open source under the MIT licence. If you want to see the loop end to end, pnpm demo signs a receipt, batches it, verifies it, then tampers with it twice — and only reports success if both attempts are caught. No accounts, no network, no prior setup.

Verifiable AI: How Tamper-Evident Receipts Can Protect Your Business From the Next AI Failure

#9857. U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

#9856. Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types)

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.
